title: Same hours, different calendar
hook: Three hours in one block or across three days: what changes a month later?

knows: reading short labels and comparing simple counts
doesNotKnow: that spreading the same study hours across several days generally leads to better recall weeks later than one long block, even when the long block feels as good or better the next day

misconception: Equal study hours imply equal long-term recall regardless of calendar.
objective: Separate the research-supported spacing effect from invented memory curves.

claims.text: Scenario, hook and prediction: Three hours in one block or across three days: what changes a month later? Same 3 hours of rereading. A month later, which plan remembers more? Options: Plan A / Plan B / About the same: same 3 hours. Correct option: Plan B. Stage labels: A: 3 hours on day 0; B: 1 hour on each of 3 days (days −2, −1 and 0). Both plans do the same activity, rereading, for the same total time; neither has a recall step, so only the calendar differs. All labels, days and durations are stipulated exercise data.

The keyed option rests on claims c5 (research) and c3 (what the toy model shows). claims.source: Cepeda et al. claims.text: Every displayed result is computed from the visible exercise state by a toy model: right after the last hour (day 0) A shows 93% and B 90%; a month later (day 30) A shows 23% and B 37%; the Day slider shows both plans at the chosen day (0 to 30). Illustrative toy numbers, not a forecast of your memory. The reveal quotes the two tests the learner ran and never translates them into a personal memory benefit.
claims.source: src/demos/lifehacks/spaced-beats-cram/model.ts (pure, deterministic; chosen constants, no fit to data). Plan A sessions at days −2/24, −1/24 and 0 (three consecutive hours on day 0); plan B at days −2, −1 and 0. Each one-hour session sets m ← m + 0.6(1 − m). Recall fades as hold(dt) = (1 + dt/τ)^−0.75, τ starting at 5 days. A session that follows forgetting slows the fade: τ ← τ·(1 + 6·(1 − hold(gap))). Values, rounded as on the stage: day 0 A 93 / B 90; day 1 A 82 / B 85; day 2 A 74 / B 81; day 7 A 50 / B 65; day 28 A 24 / B 38; day 30 A 23 / B 37. The crossover falls between day 0 and day 1 only because of these chosen constants; the research (c5) gives the direction, not the timing or the sizes. Curves, cursor and test markers are hidden before the prediction; the locked stage shows only the two calendars and axes. The reveal's numbers appear only after both test milestones and stay on the two test buttons.

claims.text: Studies of verbal recall show the same shape: massed study can tie or win on an immediate test, while spacing usually wins after a delay.
claims.source: Smith & Scarf (2017), Spacing Repetitions Over Long Timescales: A Review and a Reconsolidation Explanation, Frontiers in Psychology 8:962, DOI 10.3389/fpsyg.2017.00962, full text https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5476736/ (opened by the builder 2026-10-15). Passages: Bloom and Shuell (1981) 'compared a spaced group that studied French words on 3 consecutive days to a massed group that studied French words all in the same day. On an immediate test conducted to assess learning, the spaced and massed groups were equivalent, but on a retention test 4 days later the spaced group's performance was superior'; and 'at very short retention intervals massing is better than or equal to spacing (Cepeda et al., 2006; Maddox, 2016)'. The same review lists Rawson and Kintsch (2005), Rereading effects depend on time of test, J Educ Psychol 97(1), 70-80, DOI 10.1037/0022-0663.97.1.70, among studies where the best spacing depends on the retention delay. Cepeda et al. (2006) and Rawson & Kintsch (2005) themselves were not opened (pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov and eric.ed.gov return proxy 403 from here); they are cited through Smith & Scarf. 'Usually' is the hedge: the claim is about the direction of the effect, not its size.
claims.note: FC pass 50 (fact-checker, 2026-10-15): VERIFIED. Opened Smith & Scarf (2017), Front Psychol 8:962, PMC5476736, full text via the PMC OAI API. The section 'Language and Verbal Tasks / Adults' opens: 'Unlike skill-related tasks, for language tasks spacing leads to equal or worse learning but enhanced retention.' That sentence is the review's own synthesis and carries the claim directly (massed can tie or win on an immediate test, spacing wins after a delay; 'usually' is a fair hedge). The Bloom and Shuell (1981) passage is quoted accurately. Second-hand citations: the source string says plainly that Cepeda et al. (2006) and Rawson and Kintsch (2005) were not opened and are cited through Smith & Scarf. It does not say the same for Bloom and Shuell (1981), which was not opened either; the passage is the review's description of it. Two source fixes for demo-builder (not blocking): (a) add 'Bloom and Shuell (1981) is cited as described by Smith & Scarf; not opened' and quote the section's topic sentence above; (b) the quoted 'at very short retention intervals massing is better than or equal to spacing (Cepeda et al., 2006; Maddox, 2016)' is cut mid-sentence: in full it ends 'is true for adults but not for children'. The cut does not change the meaning for adult learners, but the record should quote the whole sentence. | v2 (W-1075, demo-builder, 2026-10-15): text and/or support rewritten for the r11 learner review (company/reviews/spaced-beats-cram/2026-10-15-learner-adult-beginner-r11.md); reset to unverified. Not checked by the builder.

claims.text: One explanation: each later session reminds you of something half-forgotten, and that strengthens memory more than rereading what is still fresh.
claims.source: Benjamin & Tullis (2010), What makes distributed practice effective?, Cognitive Psychology 61(3), 228-247, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2930147/ (opened by the builder 2026-10-15). Abstract: they 'recommend an alternative approach based on the idea that some study events remind learners of other study events'. Model section: 'The act of retrieval potentiates memory, and the degree to which it does so is positively related to the difficulty of the retrieval. That is, successful reminding following either a high degree of forgetting or a low amount of reminding potential enhances memory more for the retrieved information than would a reminding following little forgetting or high reminding potential.' 'One explanation' is the hedge: this is one theory of the spacing effect (the paper reviews encoding-variability accounts as the main alternative), not a settled mechanism. The toy model in model.ts uses the same idea (a session after more forgetting slows the fade more); the stage does not test it.
claims.note: FC pass 50 (fact-checker, 2026-10-15): VERIFIED. Opened Benjamin & Tullis (2010), 'What makes distributed practice effective?', Cogn Psychol 61(3): 228-247, PMC2930147, full text via the PMC OAI API. Both quotes in the source are exact: the abstract's 'recommend an alternative approach based on the idea that some study events remind learners of other study events', and the model section's 'successful reminding following either a high degree of forgetting or a low amount of reminding potential enhances memory more for the retrieved information than would a reminding following little forgetting or high reminding potential.' The stage sentence ('each later session reminds you of something half-forgotten, and that strengthens memory more than rereading what is still fresh') is a fair plain-language reading. 'Half-forgotten' keeps the paper's condition that the reminding succeeds. 'One explanation' is the right hedge: the paper presents the reminding account against encoding-variability theories, so it is one theory and not a consensus (Smith & Scarf 2017 also says 'a consensus is yet to be reached regarding the mechanism(s)'). | New in v2 (W-1075, demo-builder, 2026-10-15): the reveal's reason sentence, asked for by the r11 learner review. Not checked by the builder.

claims.text: Research on verbal recall generally favours spreading the same study time across sessions; total hours alone do not decide later recall.
claims.source: Cepeda et al. (2006), Distributed practice in verbal recall tasks, Psychological Bulletin 132(3), 354–380, DOI 10.1037/0033-2909.132.3.354, author abstract via https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16719566/ retrieved 2026-10-13; 839 assessments in 317 experiments. Rawson & Kintsch (2005), Rereading Effects Depend on Time of Test, JEP 97(1), 70–80, DOI 10.1037/0022-0663.97.1.70, author abstract search record https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ688037 retrieved 2026-10-13 (direct page timed out). Retrieval line supported separately by Roediger & Karpicke (2006), Test-Enhanced Learning, Psychological Science 17(3), 249–255, DOI 10.1111/j.1467-9280.2006.01693.x; publisher abstract retrieved 2026-10-13: https://www.psychologicalscience.org/journals/psychological-science/j.1467-9280.2006.01693.x/ . Prose-passage experiments found delayed retention advantages for retrieval over restudy. This short exercise does not establish that effect for the learner. Scenario values in the recall question are stipulated. Recall patch by learning-designer (session 2, 2026-10-14), applied by session 1. FC LH-3B (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): left unverified because the source could not be opened. The egress policy blocks pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov, eutils.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov and the evullab.org author PDF (proxy 403). Search-result snippets agree with the cited abstract (839 assessments, 317 experiments, 184 articles; spacing benefits verbal recall; ISI and retention interval act jointly). The keyed option is the only one consistent with the source as cited, and the why is hedged ("generally"). Re-check from a connected host. See company/reviews/lifehacks-200/fact-check-LH3-2026-10-14.md (Batch B). | FC pass 35 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): HELD UNVERIFIED. The recall why ('Research on verbal recall generally favours spreading the same study time across sessions') is an empirical claim. It rests on Cepeda et al. 2006 (and Rawson & Kintsch 2005), and no abstract or full text could be opened (WebFetch DNS failure, proxy 403). The keyed option is consistent with the claim as cited, but the claim itself is unchecked. Left unverified. | FC pass 38 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): HELD. Cepeda et al. 2006 and Rawson and Kintsch 2005 not opened. Partial corroboration from an opened source: OpenStax Psychology 2e section 8.4 'Ways to Enhance Memory' (raw GitHub module m82216) advises 'Use distributed practice: Study across time in short durations rather than trying to cram'. That is advice, not a report of research on verbal recall, so it does not carry 'Research on verbal recall generally favours'. Builder option: cite OpenStax and reword to what it says.
claims.note: FC pass 41 (fact-checker, 2026-10-15): VERIFIED. Opened on PMC: Benjamin and Tullis (2010), 'What makes distributed practice effective?', Cogn Psychol 61(3): 228-247 (PMC2930147). Abstract: 'The advantages provided to memory by the distribution of multiple practice or study opportunities are among the most powerful effects in memory research.' Introduction: 'The effects of distributing practice are extremely robust and cross-cutting: the advantages are evident in basic memory tasks using words (Cepeda, Pashler, Vul, Wixted, & Rohrer, 2006 ...)'. Kornmeier et al. (2014), PLoS One 9(3): e90656 (PMC3946552), shows the same spacing pattern in verbal paired-associate learning. The why ('generally favours spreading the same study time across sessions; total hours alone do not decide later recall') is hedged and matches. Cepeda et al. 2006 itself is still not opened; the basis is the two PMC papers.

recall.question: You have four hours to learn vocabulary for a test in two weeks. Which plan fits the research this lesson summarises?
options: Four one-hour sessions on different days
One four-hour session the night before
Any split works; only total hours count
recall.why: Research on verbal recall generally favours spreading the same study time across sessions; total hours alone do not decide later recall.
